entries.meaning: To ask God's favor on someone or something, to make something holy, or — in the passive — to be lucky enough to have something good.
examples: The priest blessed the fleet on the first Sunday in June.
Her mother blesses the children before every long trip.
The bishop had blessed the building long before the first class met in it.
A rabbi came to bless the new sanctuary.
They blessed the ground before a single shovel went in.
That chapel has been blessed by three different bishops.
We have been blessed with patient neighbors.
He was blessed with a good ear and no patience at all.
Bless you — that is exactly what I needed today.
Bless her heart, she tried to fix the sink herself and made it worse.

senses.head: Ask God's favor on
body: The core religious sense: a priest, a parent, or a speaker calls down protection or good fortune on a person. Neutral in American English and common well outside church. (благословлять)
examples: The priest blessed the fleet on the first Sunday in June.
Her mother blesses the children before every long trip.
The bishop had blessed the building long before the first class met in it.

senses.head: Consecrate, make holy
body: Used of objects, water, buildings, and ground rather than of people; the thing becomes sacred or set apart. (освящать)
examples: A rabbi came to bless the new sanctuary.
They blessed the ground before a single shovel went in.
That chapel has been blessed by three different bishops.

senses.head: Be blessed with
body: Passive only, and usually entirely secular: to be lucky enough to have some good quality, person, or circumstance. (быть наделённым, иметь счастье обладать)
examples: We have been blessed with patient neighbors.
He was blessed with a good ear and no patience at all.

senses.head: Bless you; bless your heart
body: Fixed conversational phrases: bless you after a sneeze or as warm thanks, and Southern bless your heart, which is sincere sympathy or a soft insult depending entirely on tone. (будь здоров; спасибо тебе; (южн.) бедняжка)
examples: Bless you — that is exactly what I needed today.
Bless her heart, she tried to fix the sink herself and made it worse.

entries.register: everyday — an American blesses food, sneezes, and hearts without thinking about it
entries.contrast: The verb form is one syllable, /blɛst/, but the adjective spelled the same way is two: /ˈblɛsɪd/. The priest blessed the boats is /blɛst/; a blessed relief and a blessed event are /ˈblɛsɪd/. The spelling blest is not an error, just archaic — keep it for hymns and leave it out of prose.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: the priest, the parent, or the speaker does something (blesses the fleet, blessed the ground). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory, whether a person, an object, or a place: she blesses the children, ✗ her mother blesses is incomplete. The interjection bless you is a fixed fragment, not an ordinary intransitive.
entries.passive: yes — the ground was blessed before a single shovel went in, that chapel has been blessed by three bishops. Sense 3 exists only in the passive: we have been blessed with patient neighbors, with no active ✗ something blessed us with neighbors.

entries.meaning: To be on fire or destroy by fire, and by extension to scorch, sting, consume fuel, or be consumed by a strong feeling.
examples: Dry pine burns fast and throws sparks.
Vandals burned the shed to the ground.
The barn has burned twice since the family bought the place.
I burned the first batch of cookies and started over.
Don't let the sauce burn while you set the table.
She has burned every pot in this kitchen at least once.
He burned his hand on the oven rack.
Steam had burned her wrist before she got the lid off.
I burn in about fifteen minutes without sunscreen.
His shoulders burned on the very first day of the trip.
The old furnace burns about a gallon an hour.
We burned half the budget on the first prototype.
She has burned through three phone chargers this year.
The smoke burned my eyes all the way down the trail.
My throat has burned since the fire started.
That pepper will burn for a good ten minutes.
Her face burned when they read the letter out loud.
Kids burn with curiosity at that age.
He has burned with resentment about that promotion for two years.
Nurses burn out fastest in their third year.
The porch light burned out again.
Two of the residents have burned out and left medicine entirely.
Investors got burned when the company folded.
I have been burned by contractors twice, so I ask for references now.
He burned the whole album onto a CD for the drive.
I have burned a backup disc for every project since that crash.

senses.head: Be on fire; destroy by fire
body: Works in both directions: the thing burns, or someone burns it. The literal sense that every other one grows out of. (гореть; сжигать)
examples: Dry pine burns fast and throws sparks.
Vandals burned the shed to the ground.
The barn has burned twice since the family bought the place.

senses.head: Scorch food, overcook
body: Of food left too long on heat, and of the cook who left it there. Nothing is on fire — the food is just ruined. (подгорать; сжечь (еду))
examples: I burned the first batch of cookies and started over.
Don't let the sauce burn while you set the table.
She has burned every pot in this kitchen at least once.

senses.head: Injure with heat or chemicals
body: Of skin damaged by heat, steam, acid, or friction. Often reflexive or with a body part as object — burn yourself, burn your hand. (обжечь(ся))
examples: He burned his hand on the oven rack.
Steam had burned her wrist before she got the lid off.

senses.head: Redden in the sun
body: Intransitive, of skin or of a person in strong sun. Tan is what happens when you don't burn. (обгорать на солнце)
examples: I burn in about fifteen minutes without sunscreen.
His shoulders burned on the very first day of the trip.

senses.head: Use as fuel; use up
body: Of fuel, calories, money, and time — the resource is consumed. Burn through stresses how fast it goes. (сжигать (топливо); расходовать)
examples: The old furnace burns about a gallon an hour.
We burned half the budget on the first prototype.
She has burned through three phone chargers this year.

senses.head: Sting, feel hot
body: Of a body part or a strong taste producing a hot, painful sensation. No injury is implied. (жечь, саднить)
examples: The smoke burned my eyes all the way down the trail.
My throat has burned since the fire started.
That pepper will burn for a good ten minutes.

senses.head: Be consumed by a feeling
body: Burn with shame, anger, or curiosity; also be burning to do something, meaning impatient. Literary but still current. (гореть (от стыда, гнева, желания))
examples: Her face burned when they read the letter out loud.
Kids burn with curiosity at that age.
He has burned with resentment about that promotion for two years.

senses.head: Burn out
body: Of a bulb, motor, or fuse: stop working for good. Of a person: collapse from sustained overwork — the source of the noun burnout. (перегореть; выгореть (о человеке))
examples: Nurses burn out fastest in their third year.
The porch light burned out again.
Two of the residents have burned out and left medicine entirely.

senses.head: Get burned (be cheated)
body: Informal and figurative, almost always passive: to be cheated, betrayed, or badly hurt by trusting someone or something. (обжечься, погореть (обмануться))
examples: Investors got burned when the company folded.
I have been burned by contractors twice, so I ask for references now.

senses.head: Copy data to a disc
body: To write files to a CD or DVD. Peak-2005 vocabulary and fading with the hardware, but still instantly understood. (записывать (диск))
examples: He burned the whole album onto a CD for the drive.
I have burned a backup disc for every project since that crash.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: American English writes burned for the verb — the toast burned, I have burned my hand. Burnt is the British past and participle, but it does survive in American English as an adjective sitting in front of a noun: burnt toast, burnt orange, burnt sugar. So an American burns the toast and then throws out the burnt toast.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative: the same event runs both ways (the shed burned / vandals burned the shed). Not stative and not linking, though burn with shame takes a prepositional complement rather than an object.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when the thing itself is alight or reddening (dry pine burns fast, I burn in fifteen minutes, the bulb burned out), transitive when someone or something consumes it (they burned the shed, he burned his hand, the furnace burns a gallon an hour).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the shed was burned to the ground, a backup disc has been burned for every project. Sense 9 is essentially passive-only: investors got burned, I have been burned by contractors twice. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ fifteen minutes is burned in by me.
entries.phrasal verbs: burn down · burn off · burn out · burn through · burn up

entries.meaning: Of skin, to crack and turn sore in cold or dry air; in older use, to split or crack open generally.
examples: Wind like this chaps your face in ten minutes.
My hands chapped badly the first winter we lived in Minnesota.
His lips have chapped every January since he was a kid.
By March her knuckles had chapped and split open.
Drought will chap bare ground faster than anyone expects.
The clay chapped into plates all across the riverbed.

senses.head: Of skin, crack and redden
body: Both ways: skin chaps, or wind and cold chap it. In modern American English the verb lives mostly in its participle used as an adjective — chapped lips, chapped hands. (трескаться (о коже))
examples: Wind like this chaps your face in ten minutes.
My hands chapped badly the first winter we lived in Minnesota.
His lips have chapped every January since he was a kid.
By March her knuckles had chapped and split open.

senses.head: Split, crack open
body: The wider old sense, of dry ground, wood, or paint rather than skin. Archaic outside dialect; you will meet it only in older writing. (трескаться, раскалываться)
examples: Drought will chap bare ground faster than anyone expects.
The clay chapped into plates all across the riverbed.

entries.register: everyday — chapped lips is ordinary winter talk, though the verb rarely appears outside that participle
entries.contrast: In modern American English this verb lives mostly in its participle, used as an adjective about skin: chapped lips, chapped hands. The old spelling chapt is dead. Do not confuse the verb with the British noun chap meaning "a man," which has no verb forms at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative like burn: skin chaps, or wind chaps it. No stative or linking use; the very common chapped in chapped lips is the participle doing adjective duty.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with the skin or surface as subject (my hands chapped badly, the clay chapped into plates), transitive with the cold or the weather as subject (wind like this chaps your face).
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical but rare, because the participle is normally an adjective instead: her knuckles were chapped is read as a state, not as an event, and the agentive her face was chapped by the wind is possible but stiff. No passive of the intransitive ✗ it was chapped by my hands.

entries.meaning: To strike your palms together in applause, and by extension to slap someone in friendly greeting or to put something somewhere abruptly.
examples: The whole room claps at the end of every set.
She clapped until her hands stung.
The audience has clapped through six straight curtain calls.
He clapped me on the shoulder and walked off without a word.
Coaches clap their players on the back after a bad inning too.
She clapped a hand over her mouth before the laugh got out.
They had clapped him in jail before his lawyer even heard about it.
The minute she clapped eyes on the house she wanted it.
I had never clapped eyes on the man before that morning.

senses.head: Applaud
body: The everyday sense. Intransitive, or with for — they clapped for her; you clap a performance, not a person, when the verb is transitive. (хлопать в ладоши, аплодировать)
examples: The whole room claps at the end of every set.
She clapped until her hands stung.
The audience has clapped through six straight curtain calls.

senses.head: Clap someone on the back
body: Almost always clap someone on the back or on the shoulder — a hearty gesture of congratulation, never aggression. (хлопнуть (по плечу, по спине))
examples: He clapped me on the shoulder and walked off without a word.
Coaches clap their players on the back after a bad inning too.

senses.head: Put abruptly or forcefully
body: Sudden, forceful placement: clap a hand over someone's mouth, clap on the brakes, or the old clap him in irons. The speed is the point. (рывком приложить; засадить (в тюрьму))
examples: She clapped a hand over her mouth before the laugh got out.
They had clapped him in jail before his lawyer even heard about it.

senses.head: Clap eyes on
body: Informal fixed phrase about a first or only sighting, and common in the negative: I've never clapped eyes on him. (увидеть, встретить (впервые))
examples: The minute she clapped eyes on the house she wanted it.
I had never clapped eyes on the man before that morning.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Clapped is the only form in modern American English; the clapt on the original list is a seventeenth-century spelling. The ending is pronounced /t/, which is what put the -t spelling there in the first place, but it is never written that way now.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, and abrupt by definition (clapped a hand over her mouth). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the applause sense, alone or with for (the whole room claps, they clapped for her), transitive elsewhere: clapped me on the shoulder, clapped a hand over her mouth, clapped him in jail, clapped eyes on the house.
entries.passive: restricted — fine where a person is affected: he was clapped in jail before his lawyer heard about it, players get clapped on the back after a bad inning. The applause sense has no passive (intransitive), and the idiom resists one: ✗ eyes were clapped on the house.

entries.meaning: To put something briefly into a liquid, and by extension to drop, to slope downward, or to reach into a supply.
examples: He dips his bread in the olive oil before every bite.
She dipped a toe in the lake and decided against swimming.
I have dipped the whole tray of strawberries in chocolate already.
The temperature dipped below freezing overnight.
Sales have dipped for three quarters in a row.
Ratings always dip in the second week of a run.
The road dips twice before the bridge.
The trail had dipped into fog before we ever saw the sign.
We dipped into savings to cover the roof.
I have dipped into that biography three times and never finished it.
Feel free to dip into the report wherever it interests you.
Ships dip their flags when they pass a naval vessel.
He dipped his head and went back to work.
She dipped water from the barrel with a tin cup.
The boys had dipped the trough dry by noon.

senses.head: Put briefly into liquid
body: In and straight back out again — that brevity is what separates dip from soak or submerge. (макать, окунать)
examples: He dips his bread in the olive oil before every bite.
She dipped a toe in the lake and decided against swimming.
I have dipped the whole tray of strawberries in chocolate already.

senses.head: Drop, decline briefly
body: Of numbers, prices, or temperature: down and usually back up. A permanent fall drops or falls; a dip is expected to recover. (снижаться, падать (ненадолго))
examples: The temperature dipped below freezing overnight.
Sales have dipped for three quarters in a row.
Ratings always dip in the second week of a run.

senses.head: Slope downward
body: Of a road, a piece of land, or a rock layer that angles down; also of a bird or plane losing height for a moment. (уходить вниз, понижаться)
examples: The road dips twice before the bridge.
The trail had dipped into fog before we ever saw the sign.

senses.head: Dip into
body: Two uses of the same picture, both meaning to take a little: money out of savings, or a few pages out of a book you never read straight through. (запускать руку (в запасы); заглядывать (в книгу))
examples: We dipped into savings to cover the roof.
I have dipped into that biography three times and never finished it.
Feel free to dip into the report wherever it interests you.

senses.head: Lower briefly
body: Of a flag, a head, a wing, or headlights. Note that headlights turned down are dipped beams in British English but low beams in American. (опускать (ненадолго))
examples: Ships dip their flags when they pass a naval vessel.
He dipped his head and went back to work.

senses.head: Scoop out
body: To lift liquid out with a container. Old-fashioned and regional in American English, where scoop or ladle is the ordinary word. (черпать)
examples: She dipped water from the barrel with a tin cup.
The boys had dipped the trough dry by noon.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Regular in every American register — dipped. The spelling dipt appears only in older verse. And do not reach for a vowel change by analogy with dive/dove: dip has never had one, so ✗ he dope the brush is not a form of anything.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. Transitive senses are agentive (dip bread in the oil); the intransitive ones describe a brief downward movement of numbers or terrain (sales dipped, the road dips). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the immersion and lowering senses (he dips his bread, ships dip their flags, she dipped water from the barrel), intransitive in the decline and slope senses (the temperature dipped below freezing) and in dip into (we dipped into savings).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the whole tray of strawberries has been dipped in chocolate, the flag was dipped as they passed. No passive of the fall or slope senses: ✗ below freezing was dipped by the temperature.

entries.meaning: To keep thinking or talking about something, or — in older and literary use — to live somewhere.
examples: Don't dwell on one bad review.
She dwelt on the subject for most of the drive home.
He dwells on every mistake he has ever made.
The speech had dwelt so long on the budget that it lost the room.
They dwell in a cabin two miles from the nearest paved road.
Her people dwelt in that valley for four generations.
He has dwelt in the same apartment since 1994.
A quiet resentment dwelt in him for years.
Something like hope has dwelt in that congregation through worse than this.

senses.head: Dwell on, dwell upon
body: Everyday American English and by far the most common use of the verb. Usually about something painful you would be better off letting go. (зацикливаться, останавливаться на (чём-л.))
examples: Don't dwell on one bad review.
She dwelt on the subject for most of the drive home.
He dwells on every mistake he has ever made.
The speech had dwelt so long on the budget that it lost the room.

senses.head: Live, reside
body: The original sense, now literary or biblical in American English — live is the ordinary word. Perfectly clear, just elevated. (обитать, проживать)
examples: They dwell in a cabin two miles from the nearest paved road.
Her people dwelt in that valley for four generations.
He has dwelt in the same apartment since 1994.

senses.head: Be lodged in, persist within
body: Figurative extension of the live sense: a feeling or quality stays inside a person or a place. Literary in register. (жить, таиться (в душе))
examples: A quiet resentment dwelt in him for years.
Something like hope has dwelt in that congregation through worse than this.

entries.register: everyday — don't dwell on it is ordinary speech, though the "live somewhere" sense is literary
entries.contrast: This is one of the two verbs in the group where the -t form is genuinely at home in American English: dwelt is normal in edited American prose and dwelled is the accepted alternative, not the default — the reverse of what happens with learn and spell. Watch the two senses: the literal "live somewhere" now sounds biblical or literary, while dwell on something is everyday American speech — Don't dwell on it.
entries.verb type: action in dwell on, a sustained mental activity that takes the progressive freely (he's dwelling on it again); closer to stative in the literary live, reside and be lodged in senses, which describe a standing situation (they dwell in a cabin, a resentment dwelt in him) and sit awkwardly in the progressive.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in every sense — the verb never takes a bare object and always leans on a preposition: dwell on one bad review, dwell in that valley, dwell in him. ✗ She dwelt the subject is impossible.
entries.passive: restricted — no ordinary passive, since there is no object; only the formal prepositional passive of sense 1 is available: the budget was dwelt on far too long. The residence senses have none at all: ✗ the cabin is dwelt in by them.

entries.meaning: To wrap something completely around or inside something else, or figuratively to absorb someone's whole attention — literary in both senses.
examples: Museums enwrap fragile pieces in acid-free tissue before they ship them.
She enwrapped the child in a quilt and carried her inside.
Silence has enwrapped the valley since the mill closed.
He was enwrapped in the argument and never heard the bell.
The book had enwrapped her so completely that she missed her stop.

senses.head: Wrap completely, envelop
body: Literary; in ordinary American prose wrap, envelop, or swaddle is the natural choice. Often of fog, cloth, or darkness covering something entirely. (окутывать, укутывать)
examples: Museums enwrap fragile pieces in acid-free tissue before they ship them.
She enwrapped the child in a quilt and carried her inside.
Silence has enwrapped the valley since the mill closed.

senses.head: Absorb entirely, engross
body: Usually passive — enwrapped in thought. Rare and old-fashioned, and constantly confused with rapt 'entranced', which is a separate word; enwrapt is only an archaic spelling of this verb. (поглощать, увлекать)
examples: He was enwrapped in the argument and never heard the bell.
The book had enwrapped her so completely that she missed her stop.

entries.register: rare — a literary prefixed form of wrap; Americans write wrapped or enveloped
entries.contrast: Enwrap is wrap with a literary prefix and it inflects exactly like it. It is rare enough in American English that wrapped or enveloped is almost always the better word. The old spelling enwrapt is also the reason people confuse it with rapt "absorbed, entranced," which is a different word entirely and has nothing to do with wrapping.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, the literary twin of wrap: fog, cloth, or darkness closes over something (silence has enwrapped the valley). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory, usually with in: she enwrapped the child in a quilt, ✗ museums enwrap before they ship is incomplete.
entries.passive: yes, and sense 2 lives in the passive: he was enwrapped in the argument and never heard the bell. Sense 1 passivizes normally too — fragile pieces are enwrapped in acid-free tissue before shipping.

entries.meaning: To live or be present within something, especially in a spiritual sense — a narrow word met mostly as the adjective indwelling.
examples: Theologians argue about how grace can indwell a person at all.
The doctrine holds that grace indwells the believer.
Older translations say the Spirit indwelt the apostles.
That conviction has indwelt the community for three centuries.
A quiet stubbornness indwelt every sentence she wrote.
Something like grief had indwelt the house long before we bought it.

senses.head: Be present within (spiritually)
body: Theological vocabulary: the Spirit, grace, or God indwells a believer. The finite forms are genuinely rare, and the past and participle are indwelt, never indwelled. (пребывать, обитать (в ком-л.))
examples: Theologians argue about how grace can indwell a person at all.
The doctrine holds that grace indwells the believer.
Older translations say the Spirit indwelt the apostles.
That conviction has indwelt the community for three centuries.

senses.head: Pervade, be lodged in
body: Extended literary use for a quality or mood that seems to live inside a person, a text, or a building. (пронизывать, таиться внутри)
examples: A quiet stubbornness indwelt every sentence she wrote.
Something like grief had indwelt the house long before we bought it.

entries.register: rare — theology and medicine only, and almost always as the adjective indwelling
entries.contrast: Indwell follows dwell exactly — the past and participle are indwelt, not indwelled. It is a narrow word: outside theology and philosophy you will meet it almost only as the adjective indwelling (the indwelling Spirit, an indwelling catheter), and the finite forms are genuinely rare.
entries.verb type: stative — it reports presence within, not an act, so the progressive is out as a verb (✗ grace is indwelling the believer); the -ing form survives only as an adjective (the indwelling Spirit, an indwelling catheter).
entries.transitivity: transitive — the thing inhabited is a direct object with no preposition: grace indwells the believer, a stubbornness indwelt every sentence she wrote.
entries.passive: restricted — the participial passive is standard inside theology (believers indwelt by the Spirit), but a full clausal passive is rare and the extended sense resists it: ✗ every sentence was indwelt by a quiet stubbornness.

entries.meaning: To take in knowledge or a skill, or to find something out.
examples: Kids learn the alphabet before they learn to read.
He learned Spanish in eight months of night classes.
We have learned a lot from the first two rounds of testing.
I learned about the closure from a neighbor.
We learn of most changes the same week the customers do.
By Friday they had learned that the grant would not be renewed.
He learned to drive on a farm truck.
You learn to live with the noise.
I have learned to keep my mouth shut in those meetings.
She learned the whole part in four days.
The choir has learned three new pieces this season.
Actors learn their lines before the first rehearsal.
He never learned his lesson about lending money to family.
We have learned from every outage this year.
That'll learn you to leave the gate open.
His uncle learned him to shoot before he was ten.

senses.head: Acquire knowledge or a skill
body: The central sense, with a subject or skill as object. Note that learn is what the student does; the teacher teaches. (учить, изучать, осваивать)
examples: Kids learn the alphabet before they learn to read.
He learned Spanish in eight months of night classes.
We have learned a lot from the first two rounds of testing.

senses.head: Find out, hear of
body: Followed by that, of, or about. Slightly more formal than find out, and the standard verb in news writing. (узнавать, выяснять)
examples: I learned about the closure from a neighbor.
We learn of most changes the same week the customers do.
By Friday they had learned that the grant would not be renewed.

senses.head: Learn to do something
body: With an infinitive: gain an ability, or come to accept a way of living. She learned to say no is about habit as much as skill. (научиться (делать))
examples: He learned to drive on a farm truck.
You learn to live with the noise.
I have learned to keep my mouth shut in those meetings.

senses.head: Memorize
body: With a text, part, or piece as object, often with by heart. The result is recall, not understanding. (выучить наизусть)
examples: She learned the whole part in four days.
The choir has learned three new pieces this season.
Actors learn their lines before the first rehearsal.

senses.head: Learn from; learn your lesson
body: To be changed by an experience, usually an unpleasant one. The fixed phrase is learn your lesson, often sarcastic in the negative. (извлечь урок)
examples: He never learned his lesson about lending money to family.
We have learned from every outage this year.

senses.head: Teach (nonstandard)
body: Dialectal and jokey only — that'll learn you, I'll learn him. Never write it in standard prose; the standard verb is teach. (учить (кого-л.) — просторечие)
examples: That'll learn you to leave the gate open.
His uncle learned him to shoot before he was ten.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Learned is the American form; learnt is British and reads as a typo in American prose. Then watch the second learned: the adjective meaning "scholarly" has two syllables, /ˈlɝnɪd/ — a learned professor, my learned colleague — while the verb always has one, /lɝnd/. And learn cannot mean "teach": ✗ She learned me to drive is nonstandard; the sentence is She taught me to drive.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses, including the mental ones, and it takes the progressive freely (she's learning Spanish, we're still learning). Not stative, despite naming a change in what you know.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a subject, skill, text, or that-clause (he learned Spanish, she learned the whole part, they learned that the grant would not be renewed), intransitive when the object is understood (kids learn fast, he never learned). Nonstandard sense 6 is even ditransitive: his uncle learned him to shoot — dialect only, ✗ in standard prose.
entries.passive: restricted — natural with a text or skill and no agent (the lines were learned in four days, three new pieces have been learned this season), and the find out sense passivizes impersonally in news style (it was learned Friday that the grant would not be renewed). A by-phrase is stilted: ✗ Spanish was learned by him in eight months.
entries.phrasal verbs: learn about, learn from · learn of

entries.meaning: To write a word with the wrong letters.
examples: Autocorrect misspells her last name every single time.
He misspelled "necessary" twice in the same paragraph.
Reporters routinely misspell the town's name.
The engraver has misspelled the donor's name on the plaque.
Nobody noticed that the sign had misspelled "restaurant" until it was hung.
I misspelled it on the form and had to start the whole thing over.

senses.head: Write a word with wrong letters
body: Transitive, with the word or name as object, and very often used about names on signs, plaques, and official documents. American misspelled, British misspelt. (писать с ошибками, написать неправильно)
examples: Autocorrect misspells her last name every single time.
He misspelled "necessary" twice in the same paragraph.
Reporters routinely misspell the town's name.
The engraver has misspelled the donor's name on the plaque.
Nobody noticed that the sign had misspelled "restaurant" until it was hung.
I misspelled it on the form and had to start the whole thing over.

entries.register: everyday — prefixed, but you misspelled my name is ordinary conversation
entries.contrast: Follows spell in everything, including the split: American misspelled, British misspelt. The word itself is one people constantly get wrong — it is mis- plus spell, so both s's stay: misspell, never ✗ mispell.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a single-sense verb naming what the writer or the machine does (autocorrect misspells her name). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the word or name is obligatory: he misspelled "necessary" twice, ✗ the engraver has misspelled leaves the sentence hanging.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the usual way to say it, since the culprit rarely matters: the donor's name was misspelled on the plaque, her last name has been misspelled on every form.

entries.meaning: To give a small sharp bite or pinch — and, of cold, to sting.
examples: The puppy nips at your ankles whenever he gets excited.
A crab nipped his finger in the tide pool.
The dog has nipped two people at the park this month.
A wind off the lake will nip your fingers right through gloves.
Frost nipped the tomatoes on the first cold night.
The wind had nipped their faces raw by the second mile.
We nipped that rumor in the bud before it reached the board.
Good managers nip this kind of thing in the bud.
Nip the side shoots off as they appear.
She had nipped every dead bloom off the bush by Sunday.
He nipped at a flask all through the ceremony.
They have nipped at that bottle since noon.
I'll just nip out for milk.
She nipped round to her mother's before work.

senses.head: Bite or pinch sharply
body: A quick, small bite that does not tear — of dogs, crabs, and horses, usually with at when it is a habit rather than one event. (кусать, щипать)
examples: The puppy nips at your ankles whenever he gets excited.
A crab nipped his finger in the tide pool.
The dog has nipped two people at the park this month.

senses.head: Of cold, sting
body: Of frost or wind against skin or plants. The adjective nippy, meaning chilly, comes straight from this sense. (щипать, обжигать (о морозе))
examples: A wind off the lake will nip your fingers right through gloves.
Frost nipped the tomatoes on the first cold night.
The wind had nipped their faces raw by the second mile.

senses.head: Nip in the bud
body: Fixed phrase: stop something small before it can grow. The common mishearing nip it in the butt is an error, not a variant. (пресечь в корне)
examples: We nipped that rumor in the bud before it reached the board.
Good managers nip this kind of thing in the bud.

senses.head: Pinch off, snip
body: Gardening use: remove a bud, tip, or shoot with fingers or small shears so the plant grows fuller. (отщипывать, срезать)
examples: Nip the side shoots off as they appear.
She had nipped every dead bloom off the bush by Sunday.

senses.head: Take a small drink
body: Usually nip at something alcoholic. The noun — a nip, a small measure of liquor — is far more common than the verb. (потягивать, отхлёбывать)
examples: He nipped at a flask all through the ceremony.
They have nipped at that bottle since noon.

senses.head: Go quickly (British)
body: British only — nip out for milk, nip round to a friend's. An American says run out or pop over, and reads this use as distinctly foreign. (сбегать, заскочить (брит.))
examples: I'll just nip out for milk.
She nipped round to her mother's before work.

entries.register: everyday — dogs nip, and everyone nips things in the bud
entries.contrast: Fully regular in American English; nipt is an archaic spelling. The fixed phrase is nip it in the bud, "stop it before it grows" — the past is nipped it in the bud, and the common mangling ✗ nipped it in the butt is a misheard version, not a variant.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and momentary: a quick bite, a pinch, a sting of frost. No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the thing bitten or removed (a crab nipped his finger, frost nipped the tomatoes, nip the side shoots off, we nipped that rumor in the bud), intransitive with at for a habit (the puppy nips at your ankles, he nipped at a flask) and in the British nip out for milk.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the tomatoes were nipped by frost, the rumor was nipped in the bud before it reached the board. No passive of nip at or of the British nip out: ✗ your ankles are nipped at by the puppy is barely English.

entries.meaning: To learn again something you once knew and lost.
examples: Stroke patients often relearn to walk before they relearn to speak.
After the surgery he relearned the fingering one hand at a time.
She has relearned enough French to get through a menu.
By August the team had relearned the whole playbook.
Every generation relearns that shortcuts cost more later.
We relearned the value of backups the expensive way.
He relearned the route the hard way, one wrong turn at a time.

senses.head: Learn again after forgetting
body: The core sense: injury, disuse, or plain forgetting has taken a skill away and you build it back. For changing careers American English says retrain, not relearn. (заново выучить, восстановить навык)
examples: Stroke patients often relearn to walk before they relearn to speak.
After the surgery he relearned the fingering one hand at a time.
She has relearned enough French to get through a menu.
By August the team had relearned the whole playbook.

senses.head: Come to understand again
body: Of lessons and truths rather than skills: something you already knew gets driven home a second time, usually with a note of irony. (снова усвоить (урок))
examples: Every generation relearns that shortcuts cost more later.
We relearned the value of backups the expensive way.
He relearned the route the hard way, one wrong turn at a time.

entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in writing about therapy and training, less common in speech
entries.contrast: Follows learn in every respect, including American -ed against British -t. One meaning note for the Russian gloss: relearn means "learn again something you once knew." For changing trades, American English says retrain, not relearn.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and effortful by definition; it takes the progressive readily (she's relearning the fingering). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the skill, route, or lesson as object (he relearned the fingering, the team had relearned the whole playbook), and it also takes an infinitive (stroke patients relearn to walk). Object-free use is rare but possible: at that age you relearn fast.
entries.passive: yes, though uncommon and usually agentless: the whole playbook had to be relearned, that lesson gets relearned every generation. A by-phrase is awkward: ✗ the fingering was relearned by him.

entries.meaning: To perceive an odor, or to give one off — and figuratively, to sense that something is wrong.
examples: I can smell rain coming before I see the clouds.
He smelled gas the second he opened the door.
The dogs have smelled something under the porch.
She smells the milk before she pours it.
He smelled the cork and nodded.
The whole apartment smelled like burnt popcorn.
Fresh basil smells nothing like the dried kind.
The room had smelled faintly of paint for weeks.
That cooler smells; take it out to the garage.
The gym bag has smelled like that since June.
I smell a rat in the way that contract was awarded.
The reporters smelled a story and started calling everyone.
Investigators had smelled trouble long before the audit began.
The whole plan smells of desperation.
That settlement has smelled like a cover-up from day one.

senses.head: Perceive an odor
body: The passive perception, usually with can: I can smell rain. A state verb here, so the progressive is odd — not I am smelling smoke. (чувствовать запах, чуять)
examples: I can smell rain coming before I see the clouds.
He smelled gas the second he opened the door.
The dogs have smelled something under the porch.

senses.head: Sniff at deliberately
body: The active version — you put your nose to something on purpose. Unlike sense 1, this one takes the progressive: she's smelling the milk. (нюхать, принюхиваться)
examples: She smells the milk before she pours it.
He smelled the cork and nodded.

senses.head: Give off an odor
body: With like, of, or an adjective — smells wonderful, smells like smoke. Here the subject is the source of the smell, not the person noticing it. (пахнуть)
examples: The whole apartment smelled like burnt popcorn.
Fresh basil smells nothing like the dried kind.
The room had smelled faintly of paint for weeks.

senses.head: Stink
body: With no complement at all, smell means smell bad: this room smells. Add an adjective and the negative meaning disappears. (вонять, дурно пахнуть)
examples: That cooler smells; take it out to the garage.
The gym bag has smelled like that since June.

senses.head: Sense that something is wrong
body: Figurative and informal but extremely common: smell trouble, smell a rat, smell blood. (чуять, подозревать)
examples: I smell a rat in the way that contract was awarded.
The reporters smelled a story and started calling everyone.
Investigators had smelled trouble long before the audit began.

senses.head: Reek of, suggest (figurative)
body: Smell of or smell like with an abstract noun: the situation gives an impression, and almost always a bad one. (отдавать чем-л., попахивать)
examples: The whole plan smells of desperation.
That settlement has smelled like a cover-up from day one.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: American English uses smelled. Smelt is the British past, and in American English smelt normally means something else entirely: a small silvery fish, or the verb for melting ore to get the metal out (smelt — smelted — smelted, perfectly regular). Note also that smell faces both ways: I smell smoke means you perceive it, the kitchen smells wonderful means it gives the odor off.
entries.verb type: Three classes in one entry. Stative in the perception sense — a state of the perceiver, so the progressive is out and can fills in: I can smell rain, ✗ I am smelling smoke. Action in the deliberate sense 2, which does take the progressive: she's smelling the milk. Linking (copular) in senses 3–4, joining subject to a complement rather than an object: the apartment smelled like burnt popcorn, fresh basil smells wonderful, that cooler smells.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the perception, sniffing, and figurative senses (he smelled gas, she smells the milk, I smell a rat), intransitive or copular in the give-off senses (the room smells, it smells of paint, the plan smells of desperation).
entries.passive: restricted — agentless report passives are fine (smoke was smelled in the stairwell), but the stative perception resists a by-phrase the way other perception verbs do: ✗ rain is smelled by me before the clouds show. The linking senses have no passive at all: ✗ burnt popcorn was smelled like by the apartment.

entries.meaning: To give the letters of a word in order — and, figuratively, to mean or signal something.
examples: He spells his last name for people over the phone every day.
She spelled the street name wrong on the envelope.
I have spelled it both ways and neither one looks right.
Spell it slowly for me and I will write it down.
Those four letters spell her grandmother's name.
The initials spelled something unfortunate, so they changed the title.
Another dry summer spells trouble for the whole valley.
The 2008 crash spelled the end for a lot of small firms.
That memo has spelled doom for the project since the day it went out.
Let me spell it out for you.
She spelled out exactly what would happen if we missed the date.
The contract had spelled out the penalty in the first paragraph.
Style guides ask you to spell out numbers under ten.
He spelled out the state name instead of using the postal code.
I'll spell you at the wheel after the next exit.
Two neighbors spelled her at the hospital so she could sleep.
Volunteers have spelled the crew every four hours.

senses.head: Say or write a word's letters
body: The central sense, and the one behind spelling bee and can't spell. (писать или произносить по буквам)
examples: He spells his last name for people over the phone every day.
She spelled the street name wrong on the envelope.
I have spelled it both ways and neither one looks right.
Spell it slowly for me and I will write it down.

senses.head: Of letters, form a word
body: Here the subject is the letters themselves: C-A-T spells cat. Also used of acronyms that accidentally form a word. (составлять слово)
examples: Those four letters spell her grandmother's name.
The initials spelled something unfortunate, so they changed the title.

senses.head: Mean, signal (spell trouble)
body: Almost always with a bad outcome as object: spells trouble, spells disaster, spells the end of. The subject is a situation, never a person. (означать, сулить)
examples: Another dry summer spells trouble for the whole valley.
The 2008 crash spelled the end for a lot of small firms.
That memo has spelled doom for the project since the day it went out.

senses.head: Spell out (explain plainly)
body: To state something in terms nobody can miss, often with an edge of impatience — do I have to spell it out? (разъяснять, растолковывать)
examples: Let me spell it out for you.
She spelled out exactly what would happen if we missed the date.
The contract had spelled out the penalty in the first paragraph.

senses.head: Spell out (write in full)
body: The editorial sense: give the whole word or number in letters instead of a symbol or an abbreviation. (писать полностью, прописью)
examples: Style guides ask you to spell out numbers under ten.
He spelled out the state name instead of using the postal code.

senses.head: Relieve, take over for
body: Chiefly American: to give someone a break by taking their work for a while. Related to the noun a spell, meaning a stretch of time. (подменять, сменять)
examples: I'll spell you at the wheel after the next exit.
Two neighbors spelled her at the hospital so she could sleep.
Volunteers have spelled the crew every four hours.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: American spelled, British spelt. In American English spelt is a grain — an old kind of wheat sold in health-food stores — so He spelt his name reads as a mistake rather than a variant. The phrasal verb spell out means "explain in plain terms": She spelled out the consequences.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the letter, editorial, and relief senses (spell it slowly, I'll spell you at the wheel). Sense 3 is closer to stative: another dry summer spells trouble states a consequence rather than an act, and the progressive is odd there.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a word, outcome, or person as object (she spelled the street name wrong, that memo spells doom, two neighbors spelled her at the hospital), intransitive when the ability itself is the point (he can't spell, spell slowly for me).
entries.passive: restricted — routine in the letter and editorial senses (the name was spelled wrong on the envelope, the penalty had been spelled out in the first paragraph), but the mean, signal sense refuses it: ✗ trouble is spelled by another dry summer.

entries.meaning: To let liquid or loose material fall out of its container — and figuratively, to let information out.
examples: I spilled coffee on the keyboard an hour before the demo.
Kids spill things; that is what the mat is for.
Someone has spilled juice on the back seat.
Don't fill it that high or it spills every time you move it.
The truck had spilled gravel across both lanes.
Fans spilled into the street after the final out.
Light has spilled from that window every night since he moved in.
She spilled the whole story before dessert arrived.
Come on, spill it.
Someone in the office has spilled the details to a reporter.
The dispute spilled over into the neighboring county.
Overtime costs have spilled over into next year's budget.
The horse spilled him at the second fence.
Two riders had spilled on the same corner before the race was stopped.

senses.head: Let liquid fall out
body: Transitive and normally accidental; deliberate emptying is pour out or dump. (проливать, разливать)
examples: I spilled coffee on the keyboard an hour before the demo.
Kids spill things; that is what the mat is for.
Someone has spilled juice on the back seat.

senses.head: Of contents, run out
body: Intransitive, with the liquid or the loose material itself as subject — grain, gravel, and beads spill as readily as water. (проливаться, высыпаться)
examples: Don't fill it that high or it spills every time you move it.
The truck had spilled gravel across both lanes.

senses.head: Pour out of a place
body: Of a crowd, or of light and sound, leaving a space in quantity: spilled into the street, light spilling from a doorway. (высыпать, вываливать (о толпе))
examples: Fans spilled into the street after the final out.
Light has spilled from that window every night since he moved in.

senses.head: Reveal a secret
body: Informal: spill the beans, spill the details, or simply spill it. The newer slang spill the tea is the same idea. (выболтать, разболтать)
examples: She spilled the whole story before dessert arrived.
Come on, spill it.
Someone in the office has spilled the details to a reporter.

senses.head: Spill over
body: Of a conflict, a cost, or a crowd that will not stay inside its boundary. (перекидываться, распространяться)
examples: The dispute spilled over into the neighboring county.
Overtime costs have spilled over into next year's budget.

senses.head: Throw from a seat; take a fall
body: Dated as a verb — the horse spilled him at the fence — though the noun stays alive in took a nasty spill. (сбрасывать (с седла); падать)
examples: The horse spilled him at the second fence.
Two riders had spilled on the same corner before the race was stopped.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: American English writes spilled, including in the proverb: No use crying over spilled milk. The British spilt hangs on in American English only inside that idiom, and even there spilled is now the more common printing.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and ergative: someone spills it, or it spills (I spilled coffee / the contents spill). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive and usually accidental with the liquid as object (I spilled coffee on the keyboard, she spilled the whole story, the horse spilled him at the fence), intransitive with the contents, crowd, or light as subject (it spills every time you move it, fans spilled into the street, costs have spilled over).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — juice has been spilled on the back seat, the details were spilled to a reporter; the participle is fixed in no use crying over spilled milk. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ the street was spilled into by fans.

entries.meaning: To ruin something good, to let food go bad, or to treat someone too generously.
examples: Rain spoiled the second half of the game.
One loud table can spoil a whole evening.
The argument has spoiled every holiday since.
Cream spoils fast in a warm car.
The heat had spoiled everything in the cooler by noon.
Her grandparents have spoiled those kids since the day they were born.
He spoiled the dog until it refused to eat anything from a can.
Spoil yourself — you have earned it.
Her hosts spoiled her rotten for four days.
Don't spoil the twist for anyone who hasn't seen it.
He spoiled the surprise about ten minutes early.
Someone in the group chat has spoiled the finale for everybody.
He is spoiling for a fight and has been all week.
The whole room was spoiling for an argument.

senses.head: Ruin, mar
body: Something that was fine is made worse, usually by one intruding factor. In elections, a spoiled ballot is one marked so it cannot be counted. (портить, испортить)
examples: Rain spoiled the second half of the game.
One loud table can spoil a whole evening.
The argument has spoiled every holiday since.

senses.head: Of food, go bad
body: Intransitive, of milk, meat, and produce; the transitive version puts the heat or the delay in the subject slot. (портиться (о продуктах))
examples: Cream spoils fast in a warm car.
The heat had spoiled everything in the cooler by noon.

senses.head: Indulge, pamper (a child)
body: Critical: too much giving has made the person selfish. Hence a spoiled child; British English writes spoilt here especially often. (баловать, избаловать)
examples: Her grandparents have spoiled those kids since the day they were born.
He spoiled the dog until it refused to eat anything from a can.

senses.head: Treat generously (positive)
body: The friendly version of sense 3, about a treat rather than a character flaw: spoil yourself, they spoiled us all weekend. (побаловать, побаловать себя)
examples: Spoil yourself — you have earned it.
Her hosts spoiled her rotten for four days.

senses.head: Give away the ending
body: Modern and very common, and the source of the noun spoiler: to reveal a plot point to someone who has not seen it yet. (раскрыть сюжет, заспойлерить)
examples: Don't spoil the twist for anyone who hasn't seen it.
He spoiled the surprise about ten minutes early.
Someone in the group chat has spoiled the finale for everybody.

senses.head: Be spoiling for
body: Fixed and -ing only: eager for a confrontation. You cannot unwind it into other tenses — not he spoiled for a fight. (рваться (в драку), жаждать)
examples: He is spoiling for a fight and has been all week.
The whole room was spoiling for an argument.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Spoiled in American English, in every sense — the milk spoiled, a spoiled child, don't spoil the ending. British English prefers spoilt especially for the adjective (a spoilt brat), and an American reader notices it immediately. Note also be spoiling for, which exists only in the -ing form: He's spoiling for a fight.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative in the food sense (the heat spoiled the cream / cream spoils fast). No stative or linking use; be spoiling for a fight is an idiom locked in the -ing form, not a progressive you can unwind (✗ he spoiled for a fight).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive when something or someone is ruined, indulged, or given away (rain spoiled the game, her grandparents have spoiled those kids, don't spoil the twist), intransitive of food going bad (cream spoils fast in a warm car).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the finale has been spoiled for everybody, those kids have been spoiled since the day they were born, a spoiled ballot. No passive of the food sense: ✗ the cooler's contents were spoiled by themselves — you say the heat spoiled everything or everything spoiled.

entries.meaning: To get, or to give someone, red sore skin from too much sun.
examples: Pale skin sunburns in twenty minutes on that beach.
He sunburned the back of his neck on the very first day.
We sunburn easily, so we go out early or late.
I have sunburned my shoulders every summer of my life.
By the third afternoon everyone had sunburned except the lifeguard.
Years of roofing had sunburned his forearms to leather.
The farmer's face was sunburned and lined from forty seasons outdoors.

senses.head: Burn one's skin in the sun
body: Works both ways: a person or a patch of skin sunburns, or the sun sunburns them. In practice Americans prefer get sunburned or get a sunburn to the plain finite verb. (обгорать на солнце)
examples: Pale skin sunburns in twenty minutes on that beach.
He sunburned the back of his neck on the very first day.
We sunburn easily, so we go out early or late.
I have sunburned my shoulders every summer of my life.
By the third afternoon everyone had sunburned except the lifeguard.

senses.head: Weather, redden permanently
body: Almost always the participle used as an adjective, describing skin darkened and roughened by years outdoors rather than one bad afternoon. Sunburned is American, sunburnt more British. (обветрить, задубить (кожу на солнце))
examples: Years of roofing had sunburned his forearms to leather.
The farmer's face was sunburned and lined from forty seasons outdoors.

entries.register: everyday — I got sunburned is ordinary speech, though the finite verb is rare
entries.contrast: Follows burn, with the same American preference for -ed. In practice Americans rarely use the finite verb at all: I got sunburned and I got a sunburn are far more common than I sunburned. Sunburnt survives mainly as an adjective, and even there sunburned is the more usual American choice.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, ergative like its base burn: skin sunburns, or the sun sunburns it. No stative or linking use, and in practice Americans reach for get sunburned rather than the finite verb.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with the person or the skin as subject (pale skin sunburns in twenty minutes, we sunburn easily), transitive with the body part as object (he sunburned the back of his neck, years of roofing had sunburned his forearms).
entries.passive: restricted — the participle is where the verb actually lives, and it reads as a state: I got sunburned, the farmer's face was sunburned and lined. An agentive passive is unnatural: ✗ his neck was sunburned by the sun.

entries.meaning: To throw something lightly, and by extension to discard it, mix it, or move it around restlessly.
examples: He tosses the keys on the counter the second he walks in.
She tossed the ball back over the fence.
Someone has tossed a jacket over the railing.
Just toss the receipt; we don't need it.
He tossed the leftovers without asking anyone.
I have tossed out three boxes of old paperwork this week.
Toss the salad right before you serve it.
She tossed the pasta with oil and lemon.
They tossed a coin for the last seat on the flight.
We have tossed for the top bunk every summer since we were six.
He tossed and turned until the alarm went off.
The boat had tossed all night, and nobody slept.
She tossed her hair and walked out.
The horse has tossed its head at every car that passes.
The judge tossed the case for lack of evidence.
An appeals court has tossed two of the three charges.
We tossed around a few names for the shop.
They have tossed that idea around for years and never acted on it.

senses.head: Throw lightly
body: A short, casual, underhand throw — nothing like the force of hurl or the aim of pitch. (бросать, кидать)
examples: He tosses the keys on the counter the second he walks in.
She tossed the ball back over the fence.
Someone has tossed a jacket over the railing.

senses.head: Throw away, get rid of
body: Toss or toss out, both everyday American speech where British English says chuck. (выбрасывать)
examples: Just toss the receipt; we don't need it.
He tossed the leftovers without asking anyone.
I have tossed out three boxes of old paperwork this week.

senses.head: Mix lightly
body: Cooking: lift and turn ingredients so a dressing or coating reaches everything without crushing it. (перемешивать (салат))
examples: Toss the salad right before you serve it.
She tossed the pasta with oil and lemon.

senses.head: Flip a coin to decide
body: Toss a coin, toss for it, and in sports win the toss. The noun a toss-up — an even chance — comes from here. (бросать жребий, подбрасывать монету)
examples: They tossed a coin for the last seat on the flight.
We have tossed for the top bunk every summer since we were six.

senses.head: Move restlessly; be thrown about
body: Of a sleeper — the fixed pair is toss and turn — and of a boat in rough water. (метаться; качать (о волнах))
examples: He tossed and turned until the alarm went off.
The boat had tossed all night, and nobody slept.

senses.head: Jerk the head or hair
body: A quick upward movement of the head, and always a gesture — pride, impatience, or dismissal. (вскинуть (голову), тряхнуть (волосами))
examples: She tossed her hair and walked out.
The horse has tossed its head at every car that passes.

senses.head: Dismiss, throw out (a case)
body: American news and sports usage: a judge tosses a lawsuit, an umpire tosses a player out of the game. (отклонять, отменять (иск))
examples: The judge tossed the case for lack of evidence.
An appeals court has tossed two of the three charges.

senses.head: Toss around (an idea)
body: To discuss possibilities loosely, without committing to any of them. (обсуждать, прикидывать)
examples: We tossed around a few names for the shop.
They have tossed that idea around for years and never acted on it.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Toss is a regular verb in American English; tost is a poetic spelling of tossed that a modern reader will simply take for a misprint. Its famous survival is Emma Lazarus's "the homeless, tempest-tost" on the Statue of Liberty, and even there it is doing period work. On the vowel: many Americans say /tɔs/ and many say /tɑs/, and both are standard.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and quick in every sense, from the casual throw to the judge's dismissal (the judge tossed the case). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: both, and ditransitive in the throwing sense — toss me the keys, he tossed her the ball. Otherwise transitive (toss the receipt, toss the salad, she tossed her hair, an appeals court has tossed two charges), intransitive in toss and turn, the boat tossed all night, and we tossed for the top bunk.
entries.passive: yes — the case was tossed for lack of evidence, the salad should be tossed right before you serve it, a jacket has been tossed over the railing. No passive of the restless-movement sense: ✗ it was tossed and turned by him all night.

entries.meaning: To deliberately get rid of a habit, an assumption, or a piece of knowledge you already have.
examples: New coaches spend the first month getting players to unlearn bad form.
She unlearned the accent she grew up with and later wished she hadn't.
By then the team had unlearned the shortcuts that caused the outage.
I have unlearned almost everything that class taught me about commas.
Some things are harder to unlearn than to learn in the first place.
A whole generation has unlearned the idea that the office is the only place work happens.

senses.head: Get rid of a habit or skill
body: Of trained behavior — form, technique, an accent — that has to come out before anything better goes in. The effort is deliberate; simply forgetting is not unlearning. (разучиться, отучиться)
examples: New coaches spend the first month getting players to unlearn bad form.
She unlearned the accent she grew up with and later wished she hadn't.
By then the team had unlearned the shortcuts that caused the outage.

senses.head: Discard a belief or assumption
body: Of ideas rather than skills: what you were taught and now reject. Common in modern writing about bias, education, and management. (отказаться от усвоенного, переосмыслить)
examples: I have unlearned almost everything that class taught me about commas.
Some things are harder to unlearn than to learn in the first place.
A whole generation has unlearned the idea that the office is the only place work happens.

entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in writing about habits and training, less common in speech
entries.contrast: Follows learn: American unlearned, British unlearnt. The adjective trap is worse here than with the base verb, because unlearned has two pronunciations and two meanings — /ʌnˈlɝnd/ "not yet learned" (an unlearned lesson) and /ʌnˈlɝnɪd/ "uneducated, ignorant" (an unlearned man). Only context tells you which one you are reading.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and deliberate; the entry insists the effort is the point, and the progressive is normal (they're still unlearning the old form).
entries.transitivity: transitive — a habit, skill, or belief is obligatory as object: unlearn bad form, she unlearned the accent she grew up with, ✗ the players spent a month unlearning is incomplete without one.
entries.passive: yes, though usually agentless — bad form has to be unlearned before anything better goes in, that idea has been unlearned by a whole generation. The active infinitive stays commoner: some things are harder to unlearn than to learn.

entries.meaning: To annoy or trouble someone, especially over a stretch of time.
examples: Slow permits vexed the developer for two full years.
It does not take much to vex him before his first cup of coffee.
Small delays vex her far more than big ones do.
The same question vexes every committee that looks at it.
That inconsistency has vexed editors since the style guide came out.
The problem had vexed mathematicians for a century before anyone cracked it.
Storms vexed the coast all that winter.
A fever had vexed the camp for a month.

senses.head: Annoy, irritate
body: Formal and slightly old-fashioned in American speech, where annoy or bug is the everyday word; vexing and vexed stay current in writing. (досаждать, раздражать)
examples: Slow permits vexed the developer for two full years.
It does not take much to vex him before his first cup of coffee.
Small delays vex her far more than big ones do.

senses.head: Baffle, resist solution
body: Of a question or problem that will not yield — the sense behind a vexed question and a vexing issue. The problem is the subject and the people working on it are the object. (ставить в тупик, мучить (о задаче))
examples: The same question vexes every committee that looks at it.
That inconsistency has vexed editors since the style guide came out.
The problem had vexed mathematicians for a century before anyone cracked it.

senses.head: Afflict, harass (archaic)
body: The old strong sense — storms, illness, or enemies tormenting a person or a country. You meet it in the King James Bible and older literature, not in modern American prose. (мучить, изводить)
examples: Storms vexed the coast all that winter.
A fever had vexed the camp for a month.

entries.register: formal — literary and legal; an American says annoy or frustrate, but a vexed question survives in writing
entries.contrast: Regular: vexed. The spelling vext belongs to older poetry and nowhere else. The word is formal and a little old-fashioned in American speech — annoy or frustrate is the everyday choice — but vexing and the set phrase a vexed question are still current in writing.
entries.verb type: action — a psychological verb with the experiencer as object (slow permits vexed the developer). Sense 2 shades stative, describing a standing condition of a problem (the same question vexes every committee), and the participle vexed has drifted into adjective territory in a vexed question.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the person or group troubled is obligatory: it does not take much to vex him, ✗ small delays vex is incomplete.
entries.passive: yes — editors have been vexed by that inconsistency for years, mathematicians were vexed by the problem for a century. The passive participle is in fact the commonest live form of the verb in American writing.

entries.meaning: To cover something by folding material around it — and figuratively, to finish, to enfold, or to be absorbed in something.
examples: She wraps every gift in plain brown paper.
He wrapped the leftovers and put them in the fridge.
I have wrapped half the presents and hidden none of them.
Wrap the pipes before the first hard freeze.
She wrapped a towel around her hair.
Vines have wrapped themselves around the whole trellis.
Let's wrap this up before lunch.
We wrapped up the audit two days early.
The committee has wrapped up its work for the year.
They wrap on Friday no matter where the schedule stands.
The crew had wrapped the shoot two days early.
Wrap up — it's ten degrees out there.
The kids were wrapped up to the eyes and still cold.
He was wrapped up in the game and never heard the phone.
She has been wrapped up in that manuscript for months.
I still can't wrap my head around the numbers.
Nobody has wrapped their head around what the new rule actually requires.
He wrapped his truck around a utility pole on the county road.
Two kids had wrapped a car around that same tree the year before.

senses.head: Cover by folding material around
body: Paper, foil, or cloth folded over an object until it is covered. The everyday sense. (заворачивать, упаковывать)
examples: She wraps every gift in plain brown paper.
He wrapped the leftovers and put them in the fridge.
I have wrapped half the presents and hidden none of them.

senses.head: Wind around
body: The material goes around the thing rather than over it — a scarf, a bandage, a cord, an arm. (обматывать, обвивать)
examples: Wrap the pipes before the first hard freeze.
She wrapped a towel around her hair.
Vines have wrapped themselves around the whole trellis.

senses.head: Wrap up (finish)
body: To bring a meeting, a job, or a deal to a close. Let's wrap up is standard American office speech. (завершать, заканчивать)
examples: Let's wrap this up before lunch.
We wrapped up the audit two days early.
The committee has wrapped up its work for the year.

senses.head: Finish filming
body: Film and television: production ends. Hence the announcement that's a wrap and the noun wrap party. (закончить съёмки)
examples: They wrap on Friday no matter where the schedule stands.
The crew had wrapped the shoot two days early.

senses.head: Wrap up (dress warmly)
body: Intransitive or reflexive: wrap up warm, wrapped up in a parka. Heard more in British speech but understood everywhere. (укутаться, одеться потеплее)
examples: Wrap up — it's ten degrees out there.
The kids were wrapped up to the eyes and still cold.

senses.head: Be wrapped up in
body: Passive only: so absorbed in something that nothing else registers. Also wrapped up in each other. (быть поглощённым (чем-л.))
examples: He was wrapped up in the game and never heard the phone.
She has been wrapped up in that manuscript for months.

senses.head: Wrap your head around
body: Informal fixed phrase for finally understanding something difficult, and usually negative — I can't wrap my head around it. (уложить в голове, осмыслить)
examples: I still can't wrap my head around the numbers.
Nobody has wrapped their head around what the new rule actually requires.

senses.head: Wrap a car around something
body: Colloquial American, and only in this frame: wrap a car around a pole or a tree, describing a violent head-on crash. (разбить машину (об столб))
examples: He wrapped his truck around a utility pole on the county road.
Two kids had wrapped a car around that same tree the year before.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The w is silent, so wrapped sounds exactly like rapt "completely absorbed" and like rapped "knocked" — all three are /ræpt/ and no two are spelled alike: wrapped in a blanket, rapt attention, rapped on the door. The archaic spelling wrapt is what made that confusion possible; modern American English writes wrapped and nothing else.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, literal or figurative (wrapped the leftovers, we wrapped up the audit). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the covering, winding, and finishing senses (she wraps every gift, wrap the pipes, we wrapped up the audit), intransitive in the film sense and in dressing warmly (they wrap on Friday, wrap up — it's ten degrees out).
entries.passive: yes — every gift is wrapped in plain brown paper, the shoot had been wrapped two days early. Sense 6 is passive-only in form: he was wrapped up in the game, she has been wrapped up in that manuscript for months. The idiom in sense 7 refuses it: ✗ the numbers can't be wrapped my head around.
